en: Theragāthā 16.4 Vīsatinipāta Paṭhamavagga The Elder Verses 16.4, from the Section of Twenty, First Chapter: I have reached the goal; my task is done. I am free from all fetters. Having abandoned all attachments, I dwell with a mind well-liberated. I have crossed over the flood; I am released from the bonds. Having cut off the stream of craving, I am cooled, O Great Hero. I am one who has attained the Deathless; I am one who has drunk the Ambrosia. I have reached the further shore of existence; I am a sage, one who has lived the holy life. I am one whose burden is laid down; I am one who has attained peace. I am one who has transcended birth; I am one who has reached the end of suffering. I am one who has no more future lives; I am one who has attained Nibbāna. I am one who has seen the Dhamma; I am one who has realized the Truth. I am one who has no more clinging; I am one who has no more grasping. I am one who has no more conceit; I am one who has no more pride. I am one who has no more lust; I am one who has no more hatred. I am one who has no more delusion; I am one who has no more defilements. I am one who has no more fear; I am one who has no more sorrow. I am one who has no more lamentation; I am one who has no more despair.

The Verses of the Elder Raṭṭhapāla:
“Behold this painted image,
a body of sores piled together;”
Behold this form fashioned by the mind— afflicted, full of many thoughts, and lacking any lasting stability.
With a jewel and an earring;
though bound with bone and skin,
it shines together with garments.
Feet adorned with anklets,
face smeared with powder—
enough to delude a fool.
And they do not seek the further shore.
Their hair is arranged in eight-strand braids,
and their eyes are anointed with collyrium.
Enough for the delusion of the fool,
but not for one who seeks the further shore;
it is as variegated as a new box of ointment.
The putrid body, though adorned,
is sufficient to delude the fool,
but not one who seeks the further shore.
The hunter set the snare,
but the deer did not fall into the trap;
having eaten the bait, we shall depart.
The deer-trappers wail;
the snare of the deer-hunter is cut,
and the deer has not entered the net.
"Having eaten our fodder,
we depart while the deer-trappers grieve;
I see people in this world possessing wealth."
Having acquired wealth, they do not give it away out of delusion; greedy,
they amass riches and desire even more sensual pleasures.
The king, having conquered the earth by force and dwelling upon the great earth bounded by the ocean,
remained unsatisfied even with what lay on this side of the sea.
One might even aspire to reach the far shore of the ocean.
Yet kings and many other people,
being unable to free themselves from craving, encounter death.
Having offered less than intended, they abandon the body;
there is no satiety with sensual pleasures in this world.
Their kinsmen, tearing at their hair, wail for them.
"Alas, would that we were not subject to death!
they cried; having carried him out wrapped in a cloth, they piled up a funeral pyre and then cremated him.
Thus he burns, being impaled on stakes,
having abandoned his wealth for the sake of a single garment;
yet they do not become a refuge for one who is dying.
Relatives, friends, or companions—
his heirs take away his wealth,
while the being goes toward whatever karma he has made.
Nothing follows one when being measured out—
not sons, nor wives, nor wealth, nor the kingdom;
one does not obtain long life through wealth.
Nor can one ward off old age with wealth;
for the wise say this life is short,
transient, and subject to change.
The wealthy and the poor alike experience contact;
likewise, both the fool and the wise man are touched by it.
For the fool, struck down by his own folly, lies prostrate.
The wise man does not tremble when touched by contact.
Therefore, wisdom is indeed better than wealth,
for it is through wisdom that one attains security in this world.
For because of being untrained regarding various states of existence,
one commits evil deeds out of delusion;
thus one enters the womb and the other world.
Entering into saṃsāra by way of succession;
lacking wisdom and placing full trust in that,
one enters the womb and the next world.
Just as a thief caught at the entrance of a tunnel is slain by his own deed,
so too does a person of evil nature, having passed away, go to the next world.
The one of evil nature is slain by his own karma.
For sensual pleasures— varied, sweet, and delightful—
agitate the mind with their manifold forms.
Having seen the peril in the strands of sensual pleasure,
therefore, O King, I have gone forth.
Like the fruits of a tree, young men fall away.
Both the young and the old [die] upon the breaking up of the body;
having seen this too, O King, I have gone forth.
The life of a recluse alone is certainly better.
Out of faith I went forth,
having entered the teaching of the Victor;
my going forth has not been in vain.
Free from debt, I enjoy my food.
Having seen sensual pleasures as aflame and gold as a blade, [I live thus].
Suffering from the descent into the womb,
and great terror in the hells—
having understood this disadvantage,
I then experienced a sense of spiritual urgency;
being thus pierced by it,
I attained the destruction of the taints.
The Teacher has been served by me;
the Buddha’s instruction has been fulfilled;
the heavy burden has been laid down.
The conduit to existence has been uprooted.
That for whose sake one has gone forth from the home life into homelessness— [that goal has been attained].
“Thus my goal has been attained:
the destruction of all fetters. ...
Thus spoke the Elder Raṭṭhapāla.
